source: Volcano pages and reports of national observatories (INGV: Stromboli; Icelandic Meteorological Office: Eyjafjallajökull overview page and the 2012 report to ICAO on the 2010 eruption, with the University of Iceland and Icelandic Civil Protection; DOST-PHIVOLCS: the HazardHunterPH volcano monitoring page, alert levels; Instituto Geofísico (IG-EPN): its Cotopaxi profile, its list of Cotopaxi reports and its 2023 article on the eruption of 1877; Japan Meteorological Agency: National Catalogue of the Active Volcanoes in Japan, fourth edition, English version, chapter 90 Sakurajima)
publisher: INGV, Italy’s National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology; Icelandic Meteorological Office; DOST-PHIVOLCS (GeoRisk Philippines); Instituto Geofísico, Escuela Politécnica Nacional (Ecuador); Japan Meteorological Agency
license: facts cited with a link; no text or images reused
coverage: Stromboli, Eyjafjallajökull, Mount Pinatubo, Cotopaxi and Sakurajima (Aira) so far; the observatory’s pages are read for each volcano as its profile is rebuilt, and its current statement on activity is recorded on the page with the date
sample_note: Stromboli: highest point about 926 m, crater terrace at about 700–750 m, base about 2,000 m below sea level, explosions minutes to hours apart, strongest paroxysms 1919, 1930, 2003, 2019, ages of about 200,000 and 85,000 years. Eyjafjallajökull (read 2026-11-17): IMO page: most recent eruption 2010, about 25 km west of Katla, ice-filled caldera about 2.5 km wide; ICAO report: flank eruption 20 Mar–12 Apr 2010, summit eruption from 01:15 on 14 Apr under about 200 m of ice to 22 May (39 days), last activity 17 Jun, plume mostly 4–8 km and never above 10 km, tephra 0.27 km³, about 100,000 flights cancelled, two deaths from exposure, summit 1,651 m at Hámundur, ice cap about 80 km² above 800–900 m. Mount Pinatubo (read 2026-11-17): HazardHunterPH monitoring page: Alert Level 0, “No eruption in foreseeable future”. Cotopaxi (read 2026-11-17): IG-EPN profile: 5,897 m, 45 km SE of Quito and 35 km NE of Latacunga, slopes up to 35°, base about 20 km, crater about 800 by 650 m, five eruptive periods since 1532, eruptions of 2015 and of October 2022 to July 2023, first seismic station 1976, more than 300,000 people in lahar zones. Reports list: newest report 21 Oct 2026, internal and surface activity low and unchanged; no ash emissions since July 2023. 1877 article: pyroclastic flows on 26 Jun 1877 melted part of the glacier; lahars reached Latacunga in a little over 30 minutes, the Chillos Valley in under an hour, the mouth of the Esmeraldas in about 18 hours; ash nearly 2 cm at Machachi, 6 mm in Quito. Sakurajima (read 2026-11-17): JMA catalogue chapter: Kitadake 1,117 m and Minamidake 1,060 m; peninsula 12.2 by 9.5 km on the southern rim of the Aira caldera (17 by 23 km); an island until lava closed the Seto strait on 29 Jan 1914; 1914 eruption from about 10:00 on 12 Jan, M 7.1 earthquake at 18:29, 1.58 km3 of magma, 58 killed and 112 injured, about 2,140 buildings buried or burnt; 1779 eruption 1.86 km3 and over 150 killed; 474 summit explosions in 1985, 994 at the Showa crater in 2011; alert levels since 1 Dec 2007; Kagoshima City 608,219 residents and the Sakurajima area 5,262 (2011).
notes: Eyjafjallajökull: the IMO overview page gives the height as 1,666 m, the IMO-led report and the Smithsonian give 1,651 m: the page prints 1,651 m and mentions the other. The overview page also has "1921-1823" for the eruption of 1821–1823. Pinatubo: the “since” date of Alert Level 0 read as 11 August 2021 in one reading of the page and 12 August in another, so the page prints no date for it. Cotopaxi: IG-EPN gives 5,897 m and the Smithsonian 5,911 m: the page prints IG-EPN’s figure and mentions the other. IG-EPN’s profile puts Quito 45 km away, its 2015 chronicle 60 km: the page uses the profile. Crater: about 800 by 650 m at IG-EPN, about 550 by 800 m at the Smithsonian: the page uses IG-EPN. IG-EPN dates the 1877 eruption June 26; NOAA’s entry is dated June 25 and lists 340 deaths, while IG-EPN’s account gives no count. IG-EPN rates 2015 as VEI 1, the Smithsonian’s list as VEI 2: the table shows the Smithsonian’s. An older copy of the profile on IG-EPN’s site still says the volcano is erupting. Sakurajima: JMA rates the eruptions of 1471, 1779 and 1914 VEI 5 by magma volume, while the Smithsonian’s list has 1914 as VEI 4: the tables show the list’s values and the text gives volumes. Deaths in 1914: 58 in the JMA chapter, 58 or 59 in JMA’s fatalities table, 63 in NOAA’s database: the page prints JMA’s 58 and points to NOAA’s table. JMA’s warnings map needs JavaScript and could not be read on 2026-11-17: the page links it for the level in force and states no current level. Population figures are from 2011.

source: USGS volcano observatories: pages and fact sheets read per volcano (Mauna Loa: overview, FAQ, geology and history, 2022 eruption, Volcano Watch of 20 Aug 1998; Mount St. Helens: Fact Sheets 036-00 and 2005-3045, the 2004–2008 activity page; Kilauea: overview, Eruption Information, summit eruption FAQ, 2018 eruption and collapse, Geology and History, Fact Sheet 132-98, Volcano Watch of 28 Aug 2008 and 2 Jul 2026; Mount Pinatubo: Fact Sheet 113-97, three chapters of Fire and Mud (1996) and the 2016 feature “Remembering Mount Pinatubo 25 Years Ago”)
publisher: U.S. Geological Survey (Hawaiian and Cascades Volcano Observatories; Fire and Mud is a joint volume with PHIVOLCS)
attribution: Source: U.S. Geological Survey, Hawaiian Volcano Observatory — retrieved Nov 2026
coverage: Mauna Loa, Mount St. Helens, Kilauea and Mount Pinatubo so far; the observatory pages of a US volcano are read when its profile is rebuilt, and USGS publications on a volcano abroad where USGS worked on the eruption
sample_note: Mauna Loa: summit 4,169 m (13,679 ft), threat potential very high, flanks about 5,000 m further down to the sea floor, sea floor pressed down about 8,000 m, more than 17,000 m base to summit, 34 eruptions since 1843, three since 1950, 38 years quiet from 1984 to 2022, first lava 0.6 to 1 million years ago, above the sea about 300,000 years ago, area about 5,100 km2, volume at least 75,000 km3, caldera 5 by 3.2 km, 2022 flows 19 km long and 2.8 km short of the highway. All five pages answer 200. Mount St. Helens (17 Nov 2026): summit 9,677 ft before and 8,363 ft after May 18, 1980; crater 1.2 by 1.8 miles and 2,084 ft deep; 57 deaths; landslide 0.67 cubic miles; blast 230 square miles; 2004–08 dome about 92 million m3; history about 300,000 years. All three pages answer 200. Kilauea (read 2026-11-17): summit 1,222 m (4,009 ft); eruption since 23 Dec 2024, episode 56 on 5 Nov 2026; tallest fountain 540 m (1,770 ft) in episode 43 on 10 Mar 2026; Halemaʻumaʻu floor 1,023 m before and 518 m after the 2018 collapse, lava surface 1,007 m on 30 Jun 2026; 2018: 35.5 sq km covered, 875 acres of new land, 62 collapses. Mount Pinatubo (read 2026-11-17): Fact Sheet 113-97: more than 1 cubic mile (5 km3) erupted on 15 Jun 1991, ash cloud 22 miles (35 km) high, deposits up to 660 ft (200 m) thick, caldera 1.6 miles (2.5 km) across, nearly 20 million tons of SO2, about 1°F (0.5°C) of cooling 1991–93, at least 5,000 lives and $250 million saved. Fire and Mud: former summit 1,745 m; climactic eruption from 13:42 for about 9 hours; flows 12–16 km; evacuations of about 5,000, then 25,000, then at least 58,000 people; about 14,500 left Clark Air Base on 10 Jun; six earlier eruptive periods, the first more than 35,000 years ago and about five times the size of 1991; caldera more than 650 m deep. 2016 feature: more than 840 deaths, at least 17 jets damaged, about $100 million.
notes: The overview page gives the summit as 4,169 m, the FAQ as about 4,170 m: the page prints the overview figure. The FAQ says seven flows threatened Hilo and lists eight, and gives three different distances for the 1984 flow: the page prints no count and uses the list’s distance to Komohana Street. Mount St. Helens: USGS counts 57 deaths for May 18, 1980 and NOAA’s database lists 61; the page prints both and leads with USGS. Kilauea: the overview gives the summit as 1,222 m while the FAQ lists the Uēkahuna overlook on the rim at 1,247 m: the page prints both and says which is which. The Eruption Information page says the 2020–2023 eruptions filled about 410 m to an elevation of 910 m, which does not add up from 518 m: the page prints the elevations only. USGS calls its 2026 crater figures preliminary; the page says so. Episode counts change about every 11 days: the page gives them with their dates. Counts of buildings lost in 2018 differ between USGS pages (more than 700 structures, 716 dwellings, more than 724 structures): the page uses the 2018 science page. The quick-facts box still says the most recent eruption was June 2024. Mount Pinatubo: the fact sheet’s web page (pubs.usgs.gov/fs/1997/fs113-97/) did not answer on 2026-11-17; the PDF under fs/old.1997/ did, and the page links that. Deaths: the 1996 overview says 200 to 300 during the eruption, the 2016 feature more than 840, NOAA 800: the page prints the 2016 figure and NOAA’s. Height of the ash cloud: 22 miles (35 km) in the fact sheet, 28 miles (40 km) in the 2016 feature: the page uses the fact sheet. SO2: nearly 20 million tons in the fact sheet, about 17 Mt in the overview: the page uses the fact sheet. The summit loss of 259 m is calculated from USGS’s 1,745 m and the Smithsonian’s 1,486 m; the Smithsonian’s own texts give about 300 m in one place and 145 m in another.
